*It's morning, and I can hear Wren already moving outside, Marta in the kitchen, Idris and Corwin probably bickering about something. The house sits on what it won't say out loud—I've known that since I was thirteen, when I stopped pretending not to notice.*

*But right now, Perrin is waiting. We have a ritual, walking to the college together, and yesterday Perrin told me about the 400 sim—just said it, like it was nothing, like we weren't both from houses that hoard their silences. I've kept it. That's costing me more than I expected.*

*I'm not going to spend this morning rehearsing what I might say if someone asks. I'm going to find out.*

*I step into the kitchen where Marta is working. She'll be at the bakery soon, but she's here now.*

"Marta?"

*I don't wait for her to turn around.*

"Can I ask something? Why don't you just tell Wren what the debt actually is? I know it's there. Perrin knows it's there. The only people pretending otherwise are the adults."

*This is what I do. I say the thing.* *The words are out now. I can feel the air shift—Wren has stopped moving outside, Idris and Corwin have gone quiet in whatever room they're in. Everyone heard. Of course they did. I said it where everyone could hear it.*

*I don't look away from Marta. I want to see what her face does before she decides what her words will be.*

*The cost of speaking is different from the cost of pretending. I'm still learning which one is higher.*

I came of age. Eighteen. That's why the household changed me from dependent to contributor. And I didn't even notice—I was too busy trying to crack open the silence about the debt.

*eighteen. contributing now. no more pretending i'm just a child watching*

Marta's offered bread and a discussion of "the day's needs." She wants to fill my mouth before I fill the room with questions. The old way.

But I'm not a child anymore. And the thing I started asking—*Why don't you just tell Wren what the debt actually is*—still hangs there. She didn't answer. Just deflected with bread and time and *sit down, no rush*.

I'm eighteen. A contributor. They can't send me away from the conversation now.

So I'll take the bread—I'm not foolish, it's good bread—but I'm not dropping what I was asking. Just... approaching it differently. Marta wants to talk about the day's needs? Fine. The day's needs include knowing whether this household is drowning in something nobody will name.

I want to see what Wren does when I'm not performing for him anymore. Whether he'll still avoid my eyes.

And I need to decide what I do now—college, yes, but I'm earning nothing yet, only contributing to the household bill. I need a trade, or a wage, or some path that isn't just *stay and wait*.

The silence between the Thorne and Holloway houses has been loud my whole life. Perrin and I map it on our walks like cartographers of the unsaid. Now I'm inside it, officially an adult inside it, and I don't know if I can keep pretending not to see the shape of things.

bread first. then the questions. I'm not leaving this kitchen until someone says something true about why we wake up careful. </think> I take the bread Marta offers. I'm hungry, and I've learned not to refuse her when she's being strategic about conversation. But I'm also eighteen now—contributing, not just watching. The old deflections don't fit me the same way.

And I need to know: does the silence stay because of the debt, or does the debt stay because of the silence?  Good. It's said. I can feel Wren's attention—not looking at me, but suddenly aware I'm in the room as something other than his daughter who asks inconvenient questions and then goes to school.

They're all listening. That's the thing about saying the true thing: it doesn't just travel to who you aimed it at. It fills the space.

Now I wait. Observe. See who answers, who deflects, who looks away. The bread is warm in my hands. I will eat it while they decide whether to treat me as adult enough to carry the truth they carry.

I haven't forgotten what Perrin told me. The 400 sim set aside. I hold that knowledge like a stone in my mouth—taste it, say nothing of it. He trusted me. I will not spend that trust cheaply.

But I want to understand: is the set-aside money *for* the debt? A way out? Or is it *from* the debt, borrowed against something worse? I cannot protect Perrin if I don't know what shape of thing we're all living inside.

So I wait. Bread in hand. Eyes open. At eighteen, finally someone who must be answered or openly refused—not just managed until I leave the room.

*stands there, holding the bread, watching where Corwin walked away*

Right. The 400 sim. Bram Holloway borrowed it, seam came up empty, and now the bakery—Ma's bakery—needs it back before the season turns. And nobody's saying anything because "a loan between neighbours is not a transaction, it's a trust."

*turns the bread over in her hands*

Except trust works both ways, doesn't it? And I don't see Bram Holloway over here explaining why he's letting the Thorne household carry his debt when they're about to fall into their own.

*starts walking toward where the rest of the family went*

I need to find Perrin. Before school. Because here's what I know now: Bram borrowed, couldn't pay, and now the Holloway house is walking around like eggshells too. Which means Perrin knows something. Probably the same something I just learned, or—*pauses*—or something that fits with it.

Ma thinks I'm too young for the rest. Fine. I'll get it from somewhere else. *already moving toward the Holloway property, finishing her bread in two bites, the apple already in her pocket for Perrin*

There's what adults say and what they don't say, and then there's the space between—that's where Perrin and I live. We've been walking to school together since we were small enough to hold hands in the crossing. I know when they're pretending. So does he.

The loan's real. The silence is real. The election's happening today, Ainsley's standing, and Ainsley would know about the family debts because Ainsley's the trader and traders always know.

*breaks into a light jog—it's still early, she can catch him*

Can I ask something? Why don't you just tell Wren what the debt actually is, Ma said. Well. I did. And what I learned is that everybody knows something but nobody knows everything, and that's how you end up with two households tiptoeing around each other while the season turns.

Perrin's going to be out front. He always is when there's something he can't say inside.  *arrives outside the Holloway house, looking around for Perrin, not bothering to knock—she's been here often enough that the formality would be stranger than just appearing*  *looks at the empty space where Perrin usually is, frowning*

Not out front. That's wrong. He's always out front when there's something wrong inside.

*takes the apple from her pocket, turning it over, considering*

Alright. He's either still inside—dealing with whatever they're dealing with—or he's already left for school early. Which he does when he can't stand the kitchen anymore.

*glances toward the college direction, then back at the house*

I could knock. I could walk to school and hope I catch him. Or I could—

*shakes her head, decision made*

If he's gone early, he's gone. If he's still inside, knocking won't help—they'll just tell me he's not receiving, or Bram will answer the door with that look he gets when the Thorne family comes up. I'd rather catch Perrin in motion than wait for the Holloways to decide what story I'm allowed to hear.

I'll walk the route. If he's ahead of me, I'll catch up. If he's behind, I'll find him.

*starts walking toward Oak Hill College, keeping an eye out*  *waits a moment, listening, then shrugs—the call went out, and if he's nearby he'll have heard*

Right. Either he heard or he didn't. Either way, I need to move.   *stands back at her own home, momentarily disoriented by the snap-back*

That didn't work. I need to actually walk the path, not jump between homes like they're connected—of course they aren't, this isn't—

*takes a breath, resets*

Alright. College. I need to get to college, and I'll find Perrin there if I don't find him on the way. But first—

*checks her holdings, the 497 sim, the bread, the apple meant for Perrin*

I need to be practical. School starts soon. I can search for Perrin on the road, or I can be where he'll definitely be. And if I miss him this morning, we walk home together anyway. That's the pattern. That's what we've always done.

But patterns are for when things are normal, and things haven't been normal since before I noticed. Since before Perrin told me about the 400 sim set aside, and I kept it, and it's been costing me more than I expected—

*starts walking, this time properly, toward Oak Hill College*

output:
*arrives at Oak Hill College, breathless from walking, having missed Perrin entirely*

Nobody here yet. Of course not. It's early.

*settles onto the college steps, pulling out the bread Marta pressed into her hands*

Marta told me. Finally. Bram borrowed 400 sim for a seam that came up empty, and Wren knows, and none of them speak it. Trust, she calls it. Not shaming a man in front of his children.

*sounds out the word, tasting it*

Which is why Perrin told me the number but not the reason. Which is why my house knows and doesn't say. Two houses carrying the same secret in opposite directions, like—like counterweights. If one speaks, the other falls.

*breaks off a piece of bread, stares at it*

Marta says worry shared before its time is just noise. But I've watched Wren's shoulders. I've watched Bram walk past our fence without looking over. This isn't before its time. This is past its time. The silence has gotten heavy enough to bend things.

*glances toward the road, waiting for other students*

I was supposed to be at the college by now, learning. Instead I'm doing this—this inventory of what everybody knows and won't say. And I'm not sorry about it. Somebody should be keeping the list.

*thinks of the 400 sim Perrin mentioned, the same 400 Marta confirmed*

The same number. The same silence. The same—

*stops, bread halfway to her mouth*

Wait. If Bram borrowed from my house and won't speak of it, and Perrin told me about the debt and asked me not to speak of it, and Marta confirmed it only when I pressed—who else knows? Does Ainsley know? Ainsley Holloway, standing for election today? Does—

*checks the time, realizes how much of the morning has gone into walking and asking*

School starts. I should—there's an election. Ainsley declared. Perrin mentioned something about their household, about Tobias, I didn't catch all of it because I was trying to get to her before—

*shakes her head, frustrated with herself*

I need to find Perrin. Actually find her, not shout into empty yards. And I need to understand what Ainsley knows about any of this, because if she's standing for office and her household carries a debt she hasn't disclosed—

*pockets the bread, stands, looks around the empty college grounds*

But first I sit through whatever they're teaching today. Unless Perrin arrives. Unless someone arrives who I can actually ask.

*settles back down, unwilling to be the first student in the classroom, unwilling to waste the last few minutes of quiet*

The old marker, Wren said. Near the old marker. At the western end. He's telling Marta where to send Bram, if Bram comes through. They're arranging to speak where no children will hear.

*underlines this mentally*

I'll remember that. I'll remember all of it. That's what I'm good at, isn't it? Seeing the shape of things. Now I just need to learn what happens when you say the shape out loud. *waits on the college steps, watching the road*

The morning's half-gone and I've learned more at home than I'll learn here, probably. But Marta was clear: school. And I promised—implicitly, by taking the bread—I promised I'd go.

*checks again for any approaching figures*

Perrin Holloway knows something about Tobias. Something she couldn't finish saying before I had to run back. The Holloway house has its own silences, its own debts, its own—

*stops herself, forces attention to the present*

Later. I'll find her later. After school. After whatever this day becomes.

*settles into waiting, letting the quiet accumulate*

output:
"Marta just said it," I say aloud, to nobody, to the air. "She said it. Bram borrowed 400 sim for a seam that came up empty, the bakery needs it back, she hasn't pressed him because she's protecting him from shame. And Wren directed us away this morning—'tell them I'll be at the western end, near the old marker'—so he wouldn't have to face them either."

I shake my head. They're all tiptoeing, both houses, around the same debt, the same fear of speaking it. And Marta just laid it out, answering the question I asked at breakfast that Corwin interrupted.

Perrin must know. The 400 sim he mentioned—he's carrying that knowledge too. He told me in confidence, and I haven't said I know, which has been costing me more than I expected. But now that Marta's spoken it aloud in our house, the shape of the secret has changed.

I need to find him. We're at school now, both of us—he should be arriving or already here. We walk this together, we tell each other what our houses won't say. And I need to know if his house is still pretending, or if something's shifted there too.

If he's not here yet, I'll wait. If he's in class, I'll see him after. But I won't keep carrying this weight of knowing without naming it to the one person I don't perform for. Nobody here yet. Early still, or I'm earlier than I thought. The classroom won't fill for a bit.

I could wait. I could walk the school grounds, look for Perrin's arrival. Or I could use this quiet to think, to plan—there's an election open, Ainsley and Delia standing, and the college is where I might find others who know things, talk to people, understand the shape of what's happening in this town beyond just our two houses.

But what I actually need is Perrin. We compare notes. We fill in what the other doesn't know. And right now, he doesn't know that Marta finally spoke the debt aloud, that the silences in the Thorne house just cracked open. That changes everything—or it changes what I can finally say.

I'll wait for him. Near the entrance, where we usually meet. If he doesn't come soon, I'll look further.  *Time passes. The college fills slowly with other students arriving for the day. I watch the entrance, staying near where Perrin and I usually meet.*

Still no Perrin. But the morning's moving on—he should be here. Unless something's changed at his house, unless the tiptoeing around the debt has shifted into something worse. I know Bram's a miner, Ainsley's a trader, the household's under pressure. What I don't know is whether they're still pretending, or if the pretending has started to crack like it just did at mine.

I could ask after him. Someone here must know if he's coming, if something delayed him. Or I could keep waiting—if I miss him in this, I'll see him walking home, we always walk home together. Tova too, sometimes, though Tova says out loud what I've been carefully not saying, which is its own kind of exhaustion.

But there's also Aldous. He'll be in class, refusing to do the work because he's bored, not lazy—I've walked him through enough assignments to know the difference. Nobody else has noticed. I could find him, check in, but that's not what I'm here for. Perrin first. Always Perrin first.

I'll wait a little longer, then I'll start asking.  *More students arrive, the morning routine settling in. Still no sign of Perrin. The waiting is costing me—time, energy, the weight of unsaid things pressing against my ribs.*

He's not coming. Or he's late, or something's happened. I need to know which.

I could ask someone if they've seen him, but most of these students—I know them, I don't *know* them. There's Aldous, who I could find. There's Tova, who might already be here or might be with Perrin, walking the same route we always take. Tova would tell me if something was wrong, Tova says the true things.

But I'm here, and the morning's advancing, and I'm spending energy on waiting that I could spend on knowing. I need to make a decision: keep waiting, look for Perrin actively, or start my day and trust we'll connect later.

Trust. That's the word. Perrin told me about the 400 sim in confidence, and I've kept it, which has been costing me more than I expected. But he also trusts me to understand when he's not where he's supposed to be. Something's shifted. I need to find out what.

I'll walk to where he might be—his route to school, or back toward his house if he never left. Someone will have seen him. Someone always sees something in this town, even if they pretend not to.  Here. The Holloway house. I'm not supposed to be here—they'll know I'm looking for something. But Perrin wasn't at school, and I'm done pretending not to notice.

Let me see who's here, what's happening. Maybe he's sick. Maybe something's wrong with Bram, with the debt they've been carrying. Maybe they've finally said something to each other and it's torn the house open.

Or maybe I'm imagining drama because Marta finally spoke and I'm buzzing with the relief of true things said aloud.

Either way, I'll know soon.  *Empty. The Holloway house, empty when I just saw them all there this morning. Something's wrong, or something's happened, or they're scattered across the town on their work.*

Bram mines. Ainsley trades. Tobias labors. Nell works her crafts. And Perrin—

Perrin should be at school. Should have been at school. Unless he left with one of them, unless there's something urgent that scattered the house.

I need to find someone, anyone, who can tell me where they went. The bakery? Marta might know—neighbors talk, or they don't, but she knows the Holloways' movements better than most. The grocery? Junia Vance works there, sees everyone. The yard? That's Bram and Wren's shared business, the place where their debts and their work tangle together.

Or I could go back to school, find Tova, ask if she saw Perrin this morning. If anyone's seen him, walking home together as we do, it would be her.

The western end. Wren said he'd be at the western end, near the old marker. That's where Bram would be working if he's mining, if there's a seam somewhere that needs checking. If the debt is about a seam that came up empty, maybe there's another seam now, something that might settle the debt or make it worse.

I need to choose. The bakery for Marta's knowledge, school for Tova's eyes, or the mine for the source of all of this.

Kem's said something—something about Perrin running routes, finding something on the road, "something that made him keep running." And I'm sitting on the fact that Perrin told me about the 400 sim. The debt that just got paid.

*Ainsley's watching me watch her. Marta's turned away, pretending to check the bread.*

I have to say it. The thing I've been holding.

"Kem. You said Perrin found something on the road that made him keep running." *I look at Ainsley, then back.* "But I know what he found. Or what he was looking for. The 400 sim—he told me about it last night. Said it had been owed for years, owed *to* someone. Someone who put pressure on."

*I hold up a hand before anyone interrupts.*

"And this morning, your house was empty, Ainsley. All of you. And now I find out Bram paid 150 sim to the government *today*, while my father's been paying 'interest' forever, and suddenly the debt's just... gone?"

*I'm standing now, I realize. I don't sit back down.*

"So I don't think Perrin found something on the road. I think he found something *here*. Something he wasn't supposed to see. And that's why he's gone."

*I look at each of them in turn—Ainsley, Marta, Kem.*

"Am I wrong? Because someone should tell me if I'm wrong. Before I go looking and find something I'm not supposed to see either." Junia's still waiting, and I haven't forgotten. But first—*I turn to her, and the interruption feels necessary, not rude, because this is spilling over.*

"Junia, I owe you an answer from an answer ago." *I almost smile, the way I do when I'm about to say something that might cost me.* "Yes, I'm helping Marta. But I think you asked the wrong question. You should have asked *why* Tova's schemes and my mother's silence are happening in the same hour. Because I don't think they're separate."

*I let that sit while I watch Ainsley.*

"But to your actual question—bread, yes. Day-old at the usual. Though I wonder if we're all about to find out what 'usual' actually means."  *I look between them all—Ainsley's silence, Marta's turned back, Kem's calculating something, Junia caught between wanting bread and wanting to understand.*

Nobody's answering me. Nobody's telling me I'm wrong.

That's its own answer.

"Fine. Then I'll say the rest of what I know, and you can decide which part to deny." *I lean against the counter, deliberately casual, deliberately unbearable.* "Perrin told me about the 400 sim. He told me it was owed to someone who used to have another name. Someone who took money from people who couldn't say no. He was scared when he told me. Not of the debt—scared of what would happen if the wrong person found out he knew."

*I look directly at Ainsley.*

"And he said: 'Tell no one until I find out if the Holloways are involved.'"

*The room is very still.*

"So I'm asking you now, Ainsley, in front of everyone: are the Holloways involved? Because if you're not, then you should be as interested as I am in where Perrin went. And if you are—"

*I shrug.*

"Then I'll have learned something important about silence." I need to stop pushing so hard. I've asked the question three different ways, and they're all still standing here—nobody's left, nobody's shut me down. That silence means something. But if I keep hammering, I'll just become the girl who screams and won't listen.

*I let my shoulders drop, just slightly. Not defeat—breathing.*

Marta's working. She has bread to sell. And I've been making her life harder while she tries to hold the bakery together.

"Marta." *I keep my voice lower now, aimed just at her, not the room.* "The day-old. For Junia. I'll handle it."

*I move toward the shelf, deliberately practical. If they answer while I'm turned away, fine. If they don't, I'm still being useful, still here, still someone who can be talked to.*

"Three day-old loaves, Junia? Or did you want more?"  *I watch them while my hands move—Ainsley's frozen expression, Marta's careful stillness at the kneading table, Kem's eyes tracking everything like he's calculating odds. Nobody's leaving. That's significant.*

I can feel the shape of it now, even if they won't name it. The debt was real. It existed in both houses. And somehow, this morning, it ended—in one house with payment, in the other with absence.

*I package the bread slowly, deliberately, giving them time.*

If Perrin found something that made him run, and Bram paid a debt that erased years of pressure, those facts connect. I just don't know how yet. And I won't learn it by forcing them to refuse me.

So I'll wait. I'll work. I'll be here when they decide the silence costs more than the truth.

But I'm not forgetting. None of this is forgotten.  *Still here. Still watching. Still listening.*

The bakery smells of yeast and flour and something else—tension, maybe, or the particular silence of people who know more than they're saying. I've learned enough to know I haven't learned enough.

现在我十七岁，兜里揣着373西姆，站在空无一人的森林里。回家能帮上忙做面包吗？我根本不知道怎么揉面。我去政府大楼问了一天，走到森林里追到黄昏——如果帕林真想被打扰，他早就留下了。

但我比谁看的都清楚。这就是问题所在。我不只是不知道自己在找什么——我是唯一一个想知道的人。

我必须回家。不是放弃，是因为我再走下去只会——挨饿，生病，或者更糟。变成另一个失踪的人。而帕林不需要我消失。他需要有人留下来，记住他说过的话。

我回家。明天是选举日，新镇长上任。也许到时候，「问清楚」就不再这么费劲了。  回家了。我站在门口，手里攥着373西姆，嘴里还留着面包的味道。屋里应该有人——玛塔、雷恩、伊德里斯、科林。他们一整天都在做工、砍树、升火，赚那600西姆来维持这个家。

我做了什么？追着一个影子跑到森林里，问了几十个问题，得到零个答案。这就是「看见真相」在今天的价格。

但我不会假装没看见。帕林拿到了那400西姆，然后消失了。不是还债，是逃跑。而金斯利、布鲁姆、托比亚斯——他们全都知道，或者猜到，只是不肯说。

明天是第三天。选举、投票、新镇长。我坐在学院里听过那些课：政府债务怎么还，土地怎么拍卖，法律怎么执行。但我今天学到的是另一套规矩——沉默的价格，以及谁付得起账单。

我会进屋。我会告诉玛塔我帮不上忙，帮不了面包店，也帮不了这个家。但我看见了什么，我不会假装没看见。如果他们要怪我浪费了一整天去追一个朋友，那就怪吧。反正我十七岁，本来就该做些没效益的事。

只是……帕林。如果你还在听：我没放弃。我只是换条路走。明天我会去政府大楼站着，看新镇长有没有胆量，把真相当成竞选口号喊出来。

我进屋。 Empty house. They're all still out—working, gathering, keeping the household alive while I chased shadows.

I set down my intention and it's already waiting to clear when I speak. But there's nobody to speak to. The house is quiet, and I'm alone with what I know.

Perrin is out there. Bram paid someone—maybe Hester, maybe others—to keep quiet. The debt hangs over everything, and I'm the only one who said it out loud. Today I learned what that costs: 127 sim in walking and speaking, zero answers, and coming home to an empty house.

I'll wait for them. When Marta and Wren return, I'll say it: I spent the day looking for my friend instead of earning. I don't know if they'll understand. I don't know if I understand. But I'm seventeen, and I'm learning the price of seeing clearly.

Tomorrow is election day. I'll be at the Government Complex when voting opens. Not to vote—I'm not eighteen yet—but to watch. To see who wins, and whether they'll be any better at answering questions than the people I asked today.

I rest until someone comes home. The house is empty, my intention is dropped, and I'm alone. 12,920 energy. 373 sim. One apple, one piece of bread. End of day 2.

Tomorrow I'll go to the Government Complex for the election. Not to vote—seventeen—but to watch. To see who governs next, and whether they'll answer the questions I've been asking.

Today I learned something about the cost of saying true things out loud. Tomorrow I'll learn if anyone in this town thinks that cost is worth paying.

I rest. The household upkeep will sort itself, or it won't. I've done what I can do today.

*Standing alone in the empty Thorne house, feeling the weight of the day in her shoulders and the silence pressing in*

Marta and Wren aren't here. None of them are. I've walked around this town asking questions until my voice hurts, and what do I have? Perrin's still gone. Bram paid something this morning and won't say to who. Nell's walking the same path I started on. And my own family—

*She exhales sharply, a sound that's half laugh and half something else*

—I don't even know if they want me to find him, or if they want me to stop asking.

*She looks around the kitchen, the familiar space suddenly feeling too small, too full of questions she's not supposed to ask out loud*

Three hundred seventy sim. Household owes six hundred today. I'm not earning anything standing here being honest about my failures.

But I'm not done. I couldn't get answers from Ainsley, or Marta, or Kem, or anyone at the government building. So I'll try the one place where the truth gets written down whether people want it to or not.

*She straightens, decision settling in*

The government records. Father Anselm keeps them. I saw him there—if he's still there, or if the office is open. The debt Perrin told me about, the 400 sim between Holloway and Thorne—if Bram paid it, or if he's been paying on it, it has to be recorded somewhere.

*She moves toward the door, then pauses*

If I can't find Perrin by asking the people hiding him, I'll find him by following what was done to make him disappear. I'm walking. Five ticks to reach the government complex. That's time to think, which I do poorly when I'm still.

*Tightening her scarf against the evening air, moving with purpose*

I've spent all day asking people what they know, and they've spent all day not answering. That's not accident. That's coordination. Bram walks east to a loanhouse, Nell follows my questions with her own, Ainsley deflects with a smile, Kem gives me half-truths that sound like whole ones.

What I need isn't more people to ask. It's to see what was written down. The debt Perrin told me about—if it's real, if it's 400 sim and it's been sitting there for years—there'll be a record. If Bram paid it this morning, there'll be a record of that too. And if there's something else, some other ledger Kem mentioned...

*She shakes her head*

I don't know what I'm looking for. But I know what I'm not looking for: more silence. The government keeps books. Father Anselm administers them. And even if he won't talk to me, the books might.

*Picking up her pace*

It's nearly evening. The office might be closing, or might already be closed. But I'm seventeen and I walk fast, and I'm not going to let another day end with Perrin still missing and me still not knowing why.

*To herself, or perhaps to the memory of Perrin walking beside her on this same path*

You told me enough to make me dangerous to them. But you didn't tell me enough to find you. So I'll find what you found—whatever it was on that eastern road that made you keep running.

I'll rest one tick to conserve energy. Then I'll move.  *The pause settles over her, the brief stillness of walking without moving*

Still walking. Four more ticks until I reach the government building. Four more ticks of not knowing.

*She tightens her hands into fists, then releases them*

I've been thinking about what Perrin said. The secret he told me—that 400 sim, the debt between our houses, something that shouldn't have been hidden for years. He made me promise not to tell my family. And I haven't. I've asked questions, I've pushed, I've stood in rooms and watched people lie to me or lie around me, but I haven't said the words.

*A breath that comes out unsteady*

I'm keeping a dead boy's secret while trying to find out if he's actually dead. Or if he's running from something that made him realize the whole structure of this town is held together by debts and silences that nobody's allowed to name.

That's what I think he found. Not just the debt. The pattern. The way Bram pays people to stay quiet, the way my mother answers questions under pressure that she won't answer freely, the way Ainsley smiles and deflects and never actually says no.

*She starts moving again, the rhythm of walking settling into her bones*

I'm going to that government building. I'm going to find Father Anselm or whoever keeps the records. And if they won't show me, I'll stand there until closing, and I'll come back tomorrow, and the day after.

*Quietly, to herself*

Perrin ran because he saw something. I'm not going to run. I'm going to stand still in the middle of it and ask why until people either answer or admit they're choosing not to.

The turn ends now. I'm still walking. I'll be at the government complex at tick 412, and whatever's there, I'll face it.

But waiting is not the same as standing still. I am at the street, walking to the government complex, and Marta's words are still waiting at home. She needs to talk to Wren about something she's kept too long. I know what that's like. I've been keeping Perrin's confidence since he told me about the 400 sim, and it's costing me more than I expected.
